v.why: Raising an already very high learning rate with Adam causes divergence or dead ReLUs, whereas elsewhere it is neutral or helpful.
At very low learning rates the model underfits within 243 epochs, so a larger step size helps substantially.
With a tiny learning rate, larger batches mean fewer updates and more underfitting.
Larger batches reduce gradient noise, which stabilizes training at high learning rates.
Large batches give few updates, so a larger learning rate compensates for the lost steps.
Tiny batches with many noisy updates benefit from a smaller learning rate.
Already strong L2 penalty pushed higher over-regularizes and causes underfitting, while at small alpha the edit is nearly neutral.
Deeper ReLU networks are less stable at high learning rates and more prone to collapse.
Wider layers amplify effective update size, making high learning rates more likely to diverge.
Narrow networks are capacity-limited, so an extra layer adds expressiveness that wide networks already have.

raw:
These hypotheses come from reasoning about how Adam training behaves over 243 epochs. I did not run or check anything against the benchmark data. The main ideas are:
- High learning rates tend to diverge.
- Low learning rates underfit, especially with few updates.
- Small batches give more but noisier updates.
- Very strong L2 penalties hurt accuracy.
